newsitem.title: USA: Caribbean exchanges move toward unity.
newsitem.headline: Caribbean exchanges move toward unity.

text.p: Millions of U.S. investment dollars have poured into international markets in recent years, but little of that money has found its way to the tiny stock exchanges of the Caribbean islands.

The Jamaica Stock Exchange, the largest and oldest in the islands, has seen a sharp contraction since its peak four years ago. Today, 50 member companies trade 63 securities with a market capitalisation of $1.9 billion vs. a capitalisation of $4 billion at its peak in January 1993.
"We've gone through a fairly heavy correction," Jamaica Stock Exchange General Manager Wain Iton said in a recent telephone interview from his office in Kingston.
The Barbados and Trinidad exchanges are even smaller, capitalised at about $500 million and $1.4 billion, respectively.
There is trading on the Jamaica exchange Monday through Thursday, while Trinidad trades on Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Fridays, and the Securities Exchange of Barbados trades on Tuesdays and Fridays.

Jamaica, Trinidad and Barbados began cross-trading of listed securities in 1991, the first step toward creating a regional exchange. But only two issues have been cross-listed since. In many cases, trades take place with the actual transfer of stock certificates, which can take days or, at times, even longer.

Iton is also chairman of the committee running a 15-month project backed by the Inter-American Development Bank to harmonise the stock exchange laws, rules and procedures of Jamaica, Trinidad, Barbados and the Dominican Republic, as well as to start up the Bahamas exchange and choose a common technology platform for automated trading.
"The critical objective of the project is to, in essence, put all of these markets, or as many of them as possible on a common technology platform," Iton said.
The committee issued a Request for Proposals to four companies, and expects responses by Jan. 27, and hopes to be in a position to make a selection by Feb. 3.

Backers see the harmonisation project as a giant step toward creating a unified Caribbean market that could be more of a player in world finance and hopefully, attract more of the billions invested in international markets each year.
Last year, U.S. investors put $28 billion into mutual funds with international investments.

"If there was a unified market, there would be greater liquidity in the marketplace. Certainly, it would be alot easier to attract capital for all of the various nations," said Bernard Jacobson, an attorney with the Miami law firm Holland & Knight, a member of the consortium handling the stock exchange project.

"If the exchanges can be integrated so that the exchanges in the five countries become the Caribbean Stock Exchange... that would mean that there was a greater critical mass, which would of necessity mean greater liquidity," he said.

"There would be economies of scale, and the ability to attract more investment capital, especially if international standards were being met, which they will be. The first step in getting to a process like that is this harmonisation," Jacobson said.

The consortium behind the Caribbean market harmonisation also includes the Nasdaq Stock Market Inc., the computer consulting firm Aries Group Ltd, Depositary Trust Co., National Securities Clearing Corp., Arthur Anderson LLP, Anderson Consulting and Nomura Securities.
A similar harmonisation project for exchanges in six Central American countries was completed last year.
